cards.front: Why are cells grouped into tissues rather than working alone?
cards.back: A single cell does very little, so grouping similar **specialised** cells lets them work together on one function. Thousands of muscle cells working together can move a limb.
cards.hint: Consider how far one muscle cell can shorten on its own.

cards.back: A **tissue** is a group of similar specialised cells, plus any matrix they secrete, that work together to carry out one function.
An **organ** is a structure made of several different tissues that work together to carry out particular functions.
cards.hint: Compare how many cell types it contains with a tissue.

cards.front: Which mammal tissue type has cells scattered in a large amount of matrix, and what is an example?
cards.back: **Connective** tissue. Cartilage is an example, and it supports and cushions joints.
cards.hint: Think of the tissue that gives strength rather than contracting.

cards.front: Why is squamous epithelium in the alveoli suited to gas exchange?
cards.back: It is a thin sheet of tightly packed flat cells with almost no matrix, so gases can diffuse across it quickly.
cards.hint: Think about the distance gases must cross.

cards.front: A student says a tissue is just a small organ. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: A **tissue** has one main kind of cell, whereas an organ combines several different tissues working together.

cards.front: Which tissue in the stomach wall churns the food?
cards.back: **Muscle** tissue churns the food, while epithelial tissue lines the inside and secretes mucus and digestive juice.
An **organ system** is a group of organs that work together to carry out a major function in the body.

cards.front: Why can the pancreas be counted in two organ systems?
cards.back: It releases digestive enzymes into the gut, so it belongs to the digestive system. It also releases hormones into the blood, so it belongs to the endocrine system.
cards.hint: Consider the two different substances it releases and where each one goes.

cards.front: During exercise, how do the respiratory and circulatory systems cooperate to supply the muscles?
cards.back: The respiratory system takes in more oxygen. The circulatory system carries it in the blood to the muscles, which need more oxygen during exercise.
cards.hint: Follow the oxygen from the air to the muscle cells.

cards.front: What is the order of levels of organisation from a cell up to an organism?
cards.back: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems make up the organism.

cards.front: Why does failure of one organ system affect the whole body?
cards.back: Systems depend on each other. For example, failing lungs deprive every tissue of oxygen.
cards.hint: Think about what every tissue needs in order to keep working.

cards.front: Which plant tissue carries water and mineral ions upwards from the roots?
cards.back: **Xylem** carries water and mineral ions upwards from the roots.
cards.hint: Compare it with the plant tissue that moves sugars.
